description: Plan a calmer National Day trip with a practical checklist for preparation, transport, accommodation, exploring and the journey home.

children: Fewer hassles. More of the view.
Sort out the practical details before leaving, then spend your holiday on the places you want to see. A useful checklist from packing to coming home.

props.aria-label: Prepare one step at a time

children: Prepare one step at a time
Set a total budget before choosing a destination
Add up transport, rooms, meals, tickets and local travel, with a buffer. A cheap ticket does not always mean a cheap trip.
Check dates, guests, room type and what is included. Save cancellation terms and confirmation; use official or established booking channels.
Recheck weather and attraction opening notices
Check the route and destination forecast, traffic notices and reservation rules. Keep an alternative for rain or closures.
Keep IDs, tickets, accommodation addresses, bookings and companion contacts accessible without a connection.
Arriving safely is part of the plan.
Buckle up before the vehicle moves
Use a seat belt in both front and rear seats, including rentals and shared rides.
No alcohol for the driver; rest when tired
Check the vehicle before a road trip and plan rest stops. Avoid driving through the night to squeeze in another day.
Allow for security checks, walking, luggage and local traffic. A lighter arrival day is often easier to enjoy.
Cities can have several stations or airports. Confirm the exact location, ID requirements and return booking with the official operator.
Choose a room that works for your trip.
Include travel time in the room price
A cheaper remote room can add taxi costs. Compare actual routes to stations and sights, including the journey back at night.
Confirm late arrival, children and access needs in advance. Keep the booking conversation for reference.
Locate evacuation routes and stairs. Follow the property’s fire rules and avoid prohibited open flames.
Do a quick check before leaving the room
Check your ID, phone, keys and essentials. Keep valuables secure and avoid leaving luggage unattended for a photo.
Leave time for the place—and room to change plans.
Stay on routes open to visitors
Avoid undeveloped, closed or unsupported areas. Change plans when official warnings or closures apply.
Follow safety rules on the water
Wear a life jacket as required on boats. Read warnings and assess suitability before water or height-based activities.
Prioritize the places you care about and keep the rest optional. Give yourself permission to skip a long queue.
Order what you need and take waste away
Order a little first and add more if needed. Carry a reusable bottle and follow local waste and conservation rules.
Finish the trip with a little breathing room.
Check return dates, stations and arrival times, including how you will get home after a late arrival.
Check drawers, sockets, bathroom and bedside areas for IDs, chargers and belongings before checkout.
Review charges and refund progress after the trip. Contact the provider or booking platform with the booking details if something is unclear.
Leave time to settle back in
Keep extra tasks light on the return day and allow time to unpack, wash and sleep before resuming your routine.
Choose a platform and share a small step toward a better life.
Suggestions from the book to take with you
These are original book suggestions. Marking them updates your long-term checklist, and each can be shared as a card.
Always wear seat belts, both front and back

Wearing a seat belt in the front seat cuts the risk of dying in a crash by roughly half. For drivers and passengers in light trucks, the reduction is about 60%. Among U.S. crash victims in 2022 whose seat belt use was documented, half were not wearing one.
No cost at all. It only adds about 2 seconds to every trip…

children: Wearing a helmet and fastening the strap while riding motorcycles or e-bikes

Wearing a helmet and fastening the strap properly reduces a motorcyclist’s risk of dying in an accident by roughly 40%. The chance of suffering a head injury drops by about 70%. The strap must be tightened; a helmet that simply hangs loosely on the head does not count as being worn.

children: Don’t speed or drive after drinking

On average, for every 1% increase in speed, the chance of a fatal crash rises by roughly 4%. There is no “safe” level of alcohol consumption when it comes to driving; even very low blood alcohol concentrations already raise the risk of accidents.

children: Turn off non‑essential notifications and keep your phone out of sight while working

Even if you don’t look at or touch your phone when it rings, your performance on attention‑related tasks still drops. The drop is roughly the same as when you actually answer calls or send messages. Another scenario: even when the phone sits on the desk and you resist the urge to glance at it, the amount of mental capacity available still decreases. The more dependent a person is on their phone, the greater this drop tends to be.

children: Getting 7 to 8 hours of sleep each night — don’t settle for just 6 hours

After two full weeks of getting only 6 hours of sleep each night, brain performance drops to a level equivalent to going two full nights without any sleep at all. The tricky part is that people don’t notice this effect themselves. Their self-rated sleepiness only rises during the first few days and then plateaus — people sleeping 6 hours report the same level of fatigue as those sleeping just 4 hours. In other words, the belief that “6 hours of sleep is enough for me” is actually a symptom of chronic sleep deprivation.

children: Before traveling abroad, send your itinerary, accommodation details, and travel companions’ information to a family member, and agree on how often you’ll stay in touch

If a traveler goes missing overseas, their family can turn to Chinese diplomatic missions for help. These missions provide relatives with local police contact information and other resources for assistance. Once a police report is filed, the consulate follows up to ensure timely action. Whether this support chain can be activated depends on whether someone back home knows exactly where the traveler is and when they’re supposed to make contact. Sharing flight numbers, hotel addresses, companions’ phone numbers, and agreed-upon check-in intervals with one trusted person is sufficient.
No cost at all. Simply send a message before you leave.
